stem: A rice miller maps the goods arriving from farms and leaving to shops, the orders and forecasts travelling back the other way, and the payments that follow. What has it mapped, and what flows through it?
choices: A supply chain: materials, information and money across suppliers, manufacturers and customers
A value chain: the primary and support activities inside one firm that create margin
A logistics network: the movement and storage of goods between locations
A process map: the sequence of steps used to turn one order into a finished product
explanation: Three flows across several organisations is the supply chain. A value chain looks inside one firm at the activities that add value, and logistics is only the goods-movement part of the wider chain.

stem: A cafe maps its own Order to Pay to Prepare to Pickup steps and improves the handoffs between them. Which discipline is this, as this course draws the boundary?
choices: Operations management, because the flow stays within one organisation
Supply chain management, because several parties are involved
Logistics management, because goods are handed over to a customer
Demand planning, because the cafe must forecast how many orders will arrive
explanation: Slide 4 draws the line by scope: operations manages flow within one organisation and one process; SCM coordinates flow across organisations (supplier to manufacturer to distributor to retailer to customer). The number of steps in the process is irrelevant to which side of the line you are on.

stem: According to this course, real supply chains are best described as simple linear chains running from one supplier through to one customer.
choices: True
False
explanation: Slide 7 contrasts the simplified textbook view (a straight line) with reality: multiple suppliers, multiple factories, multiple 3PL providers, multiple channels and multiple customer segments, all cross-linked. Real supply chains are networks.

stem: Select all of the following that are the enablers that make the supply chain work, alongside the actors.
choices: Marketing
Logistics
Technology
Regulation
Finance
explanation: Slide 6 names three enablers: logistics (right product, right place, right time), technology (information systems, data visibility, automation, collaboration platforms) and finance (working capital, trade finance, risk management, payment solutions). Marketing and regulation are not on that slide.

stem: CP Group appears in this course as supplier, manufacturer, distributor/logistics operator and retailer (7-Eleven, Lotus's, Makro) all at once. What point is this case making?
choices: Vertical integration always lowers total supply-chain cost
A company should single-source in order to keep unit costs down
Retailers are the only actor that touches the end customer
One company can occupy several roles in the same chain and create value across the whole of it
explanation: Slide 8 is titled 'One Company, Multiple Roles', and slide 9 adds that the same group runs several distinct product supply chains (feed, meat, seafood, ready-to-eat, dairy, pharma). This course never claims integration is automatically cheaper.

stem: Which of these is a supply-chain-level (SCOR) performance attribute in this course, rather than a Week 2 process-level objective?
choices: Quality
Dependability
Asset efficiency
Speed
explanation: Slide 11 puts quality, speed, dependability, flexibility and cost on the Week 2 process side, and reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost and asset efficiency on the Week 3 supply-chain side. Asset efficiency, the utilisation of assets across the whole chain, only exists at the network level.

stem: Which pair of KPIs measures the low-inventory versus high-availability trade-off?
choices: Inventory turns and fill rate
Cost per unit and order cycle time
Operating cost ratio and time to adapt
Cost per unit and fill rate
explanation: Inventory turns (higher is better) measures how lean the stock is, and fill rate (higher is better) measures availability. Cost per unit with order cycle time belongs to low cost versus high responsiveness, and operating cost ratio with time to adapt belongs to efficiency versus flexibility.

stem: In this course's efficient-versus-responsive table, an efficient supply chain is characterised by which combination?
choices: Uncertain demand, buffer inventory, flexible suppliers
Predictable demand, buffer inventory, capacity cushion
Uncertain demand, lean inventory, cost-focused suppliers
Predictable demand, lean inventory, high capacity utilisation
explanation: Slide 15: efficient means predictable demand, cost priority, lean inventory, high utilisation, cost-focused suppliers, commodity example. Buffer inventory and a capacity cushion are the responsive column, and they are what makes option B tempting.

stem: A retailer sells seasonal fashion items with short life cycles and volatile demand. Which kind of supply chain should it build?
choices: Efficient: lean inventory and suppliers chosen on cost
Responsive: buffer inventory, capacity cushion and flexible suppliers
Efficient: high capacity utilisation to spread fixed costs
Responsive: lean inventory and high utilisation to keep prices low
explanation: Uncertain demand calls for the responsive column: speed and flexibility priority, buffer stock, capacity cushion, flexible suppliers, with fashion given as the example. Option D is the trap, pairing the responsive label with efficient settings.

stem: On the Big C versus Zara strategic-fit slide, how is Zara's supply-chain approach described?
choices: Pull-hybrid: design, make and deliver based on real demand signals
Push: efficient production and distribution planned in advance
Pure pull: nothing at all is produced until a customer order arrives
Push-hybrid: forecast-driven with occasional replenishment
explanation: Slide 16 labels Zara 'Pull-Hybrid' under a differentiation strategy with trend-driven, uncertain demand, emphasising speed and flexibility. Push with efficiency and scale is the Big C column, and pure pull overstates it because Zara still designs and produces ahead of individual customer orders.

stem: A large hypermarket competes on cost leadership with predictable, staple demand and a push-based supply chain. Which set of KPIs fits that strategy?
choices: Lead time to store, sell-through rate, stockout rate, new product contribution
Fill rate, order cycle time, time to adapt, agility index
Cost per unit, inventory turns, on-time in-full, supply chain cost percentage
Cash-to-cash cycle, days of supply, forecast accuracy, perfect order rate
explanation: An efficient supply chain is measured on cost and asset use, because that is what it is built to win on. The first set — lead time to store, sell-through, new product contribution — is how a responsive fashion chain measures itself, where speed to market matters more than cost per unit.

stem: A product is forecast at 100 units but actual demand turns out to be 120. Using this course's two forecast-error scenarios, what has happened and what follows?
choices: Overforecast; 20 units of excess inventory, holding cost and markdown risk
Underforecast; 20 units of excess inventory that must be written off
Overforecast; 20 units of unmet demand and dissatisfied customers
Underforecast; 20 units of unmet demand, lost sales and expedited shipments
explanation: Actual above forecast is an underforecast, which leads to a stockout: 20 units of unmet demand, lost sales, dissatisfied customers and higher costs from expediting. Excess inventory, obsolescence and markdowns are the overforecast scenario, where forecast 100 meets actual 80.

stem: There are four reasons companies hold inventory. Select all of the following that are on that list.
choices: Increase obsolescence risk
Buffer uncertainty
Reduce the cost of capital tied up in stock
Decouple activities
Gain purchasing or production efficiency
explanation: Slide 20 lists four reasons: meet customer demand, buffer uncertainty, decouple activities, and gain purchasing/production efficiency. Obsolescence risk and capital tied up are costs of holding too much inventory (slide 21), not reasons to hold it.

stem: Where does work-in-process (WIP) inventory sit in this course's map of the chain, and what is its stated purpose?
choices: At the supplier, to ensure reliable supply and support economies of scale
At the warehouse, to meet customer demand and enable responsive delivery
At the factory, to keep production flowing, balance process times and absorb process variability
At the retailer, to ensure high availability and support variety and choice
explanation: Slide 22 maps raw materials to the supplier, WIP to the factory, finished goods to the warehouse and retail inventory to the retailer. WIP is items being worked on but not yet complete, so its job is keeping production flowing and absorbing process variability.

stem: A furniture maker cuts and assembles nothing until a customer has signed an order. In this course's terms this is:
choices: Push / make-to-stock, triggered by forecast
Push / make-to-order, triggered by a production schedule
Pull / make-to-stock, triggered by a replenishment signal
Pull / make-to-order, triggered by actual customer demand
explanation: Slide 23 defines pull as make-to-order: inventory is built only after demand is known, best when demand is uncertain or the product is customised, with custom furniture given as the example. Push is the forecast-triggered make-to-stock side.

stem: A furniture maker builds standard frames to forecast and holds them in stock, then only cuts and fits the fabric once a customer has ordered. What is the point between those two stages called?
choices: The push-pull boundary
The point where ownership transfers from supplier to buyer
The reorder point
The point where safety stock is exhausted
explanation: Upstream of the boundary work is pushed on a forecast; downstream it is pulled by real demand. Moving the boundary later means less finished stock at risk but a longer wait for the customer.

stem: Which supply-chain strategy is described as 'push upstream, pull downstream', with the push-pull boundary deliberately placed?
choices: Efficient
Responsive
Agile
Hybrid / leagile
explanation: Slide 27 gives hybrid/leagile the job of balancing efficiency and responsiveness: push upstream, pull downstream, segment customers and products, put the right inventory in the right place. Agile is the high-uncertainty, high-variety strategy built on small batches, flexible suppliers and postponement.

stem: A manufacturer that has bought a critical component from one supplier for years now qualifies two additional suppliers. Following the sourcing trade-off table, what should it expect?
choices: Lower unit cost and simpler management, but higher supply risk
Lower cost and lower risk together, with no offsetting downside
Lower supply risk, more flexibility and stronger buying leverage, but higher cost and more complexity
Higher supply risk and less flexibility, but lower purchasing cost
explanation: Slide 26 puts multiple sourcing at higher cost and more complexity but lower supply risk, more flexibility and stronger leverage. Option A describes the single-sourcing position the firm is leaving, which is exactly the trap.

stem: What does this course give as the trade-off for local or nearshore sourcing?
choices: Faster and more resilient, but potentially higher cost and limited capacity
Lower cost and broader access to capability, but longer lead times
Lower emissions and lower cost, with no capacity constraint
Shorter lead time and lower cost, but higher tariff exposure
explanation: Slide 28 states local/nearshore as faster and resilient, but potentially higher cost with limited capacity. Lower cost and access to broader capability, at the price of longer lead times, disruption and tariffs, is the global sourcing side.

stem: A Bangkok exporter ships bulk, low-value raw material to Europe and has made sustainability a stated priority. Which mode does this course's decision rule point to?
choices: Air freight, because its schedules are more predictable
Ocean freight, because cost per kg and emissions per kg are both lower
Air freight, because emissions per kg are lower
Road freight, because it is the most flexible mode
explanation: Slide 31: sea is low cost per kg and low emissions per kg but slow (25 to 40 days) and more variable; air is fast (2 to 5 days) and more predictable but high cost and high emissions. Bulk, low value and sustainability-led all point to sea, and this course's rule is to prioritise cost savings or sustainability by choosing sea.

stem: A retailer consolidates eight regional warehouses into two large national ones. Based on the centralised-versus-decentralised table, what is the expected effect?
choices: Higher total inventory and faster delivery
Lower total inventory and faster delivery
Higher total inventory and longer delivery
Lower total inventory and economies of scale, but longer delivery
explanation: Slide 34: centralised means fewer facilities, lower inventory, economies of scale and longer delivery; decentralised is the mirror image. Option B is the tempting one because it sounds like pure improvement, but you cannot buy both lower inventory and faster delivery from this single move.

stem: A shop sells two more units than usual this week. It orders ten extra from the wholesaler, who orders fifty extra from the factory, who schedules a much larger production run. What is this called?
choices: The bullwhip effect
The push-pull boundary moving upstream
A stockout cascade
Demand smoothing
explanation: Small changes in customer demand produce progressively larger order swings the further upstream you go. It is driven by forecast updating, order batching, promotions, long lead times and stages not sharing information.

stem: Select all of the following that are causes of the bullwhip effect.
choices: Sharing real-time point-of-sale data with upstream partners
Order batching
Long lead times
Placing small, frequent replenishment orders
Poor information sharing
explanation: Slide 33 lists five causes: forecast updating, order batching, promotions, long lead times and poor information sharing. Sharing real point-of-sale data and ordering in small frequent lots are the opposite of two of those causes, so they damp the whip rather than crack it.

stem: A distributor holds its orders back until it has enough volume to fill a full truckload, then places one large order. Which bullwhip cause is this?
choices: Forecast updating
Order batching
Promotions
Long lead times
explanation: Order batching is placing large, infrequent orders instead of smaller, more frequent ones, which creates artificial spikes in demand upstream. Forecast updating would be each stage re-forecasting independently on limited information and overreacting to recent changes.

stem: This course says real-time dashboards help reduce the bullwhip effect. What mechanism does it give?
choices: They increase safety stock at every stage of the chain
They let each stage build its own forecast independently and more accurately
They lengthen order cycles so that batches even out over time
They improve visibility of live inventory, transit times and sales, so decisions use facts rather than guesses
explanation: Visibility attacks the poor-information-sharing cause from slide 33, where limited visibility of real demand and inventory leads to guesses instead of facts, and the wrap-up repeats that coordination and visibility reduce bullwhip. More independent forecasting at each stage is itself a cause of bullwhip, not a cure.

stem: In the Beer Game, inventory costs $0.50 per case per week and backlog costs $1.00 per case per week. A wholesaler ends week 1 with 12 cases in stock, week 2 with a backlog of 6 cases, and week 3 with 8 cases in stock. What is its total cost over the three weeks?
explanation: 12 x $0.50 + 6 x $1.00 + 8 x $0.50 = $6.00 + $6.00 + $4.00 = $16.00. The $13.00 trap costs all 26 cases at the inventory rate, forgetting that backlog is priced at double; $10.00 ignores the backlog week entirely.

stem: Beer Game week 1: a retailer starts with 10 cases and receives a 10-case shipment, giving 20 cases before shipping. The customer orders 14 cases and all 14 are shipped. What is the closing position and that week's cost?
choices: 6 cases in inventory; $3.00
6 cases in inventory; $6.00
4 cases in inventory; $2.00
4 cases of backlog; $4.00
explanation: The slide's worked row computes closing stock as 20 minus what was shipped, so 20 - 14 = 6 cases, charged at the $0.50 inventory rate for $3.00. The $1.00 rate applies only to backlog, and here demand was met in full.

stem: The Beer Game rules forbid teams from talking about demand forecasts outside of their orders. Which real-world condition does this rule simulate?
choices: Order batching, because each player may only order once per round
Promotions, because demand is artificially inflated during the game
Poor information sharing, so each stage sees only the order from the stage below it
Long lead times between placing an order and receiving the shipment
explanation: The no-talking rule removes visibility of real customer demand, which slide 33 names as a bullwhip cause and slide 38 answers with real-time visibility. Lead time is simulated separately, by the shipping delay between stages rather than by the communication ban.
